title: Final Mastery Assessment and Continuing Development
orientation:
This capstone closes the structured route while keeping the course and reference library open for continuing study. It combines objective decisions, grammatical analysis, correction, transformation, paragraph editing and independent formal writing. The objective sample revisits the six broad domains used by the diagnostic, with different items and clearly stated contexts. Compare the underlying distinctions and your original writing as well as the counts shown in the report.

Attempt the work before opening feedback, and note any reference help you use. The title’s mastery aim does not mean that thirty calendar days or one strong multiple-choice result certifies expert proficiency. Open responses require reasoned self-review against their rubrics; model exposure is not an automatic grade. Use the topic profile to select precise revision priorities, then continue with unfamiliar practice and later retrieval. Every lesson and reference entry remains available after this day.
outcomes: Apply grammar across the six diagnostic skill domains and explain the limits of numerical comparison.
Correct and transform unfamiliar sentences without altering essential meaning.
Produce a qualified formal report and a faithful concise précis.
Interpret first responses, exposure, retention and writing self-review separately.
Build a specific continuing revision plan and select appropriate permanent resources.

modules.title: The capstone and a fair comparison with your starting point
modules.definition: A capstone combines several abilities in an integrated task. A diagnostic comparison examines performance in related skill domains at two points; it does not automatically establish a calibrated gain in overall proficiency.
foundation: Keep your initial diagnostic and the present responses as separate samples. Both include form and sentence analysis; nouns, determiners and reference; verbs, time, voice and modality; modification and relationships; conventions and usage; and discourse, editing and writing. The objective items use different sentences so that remembering an earlier answer is not the intended route to success. Some forms may nevertheless be familiar from study, which is a legitimate consequence of learning. Work through the context supplied and produce the written responses before consulting their models.
intermediate: A fair personal comparison begins with what was actually attempted. Three correct answers from four attempted items are not interchangeable with three correct answers from twelve attempted items. An unanswered item supplies no evidence of a correct response. Compare the grammatical distinctions behind mistakes and inspect your original writing, rather than treating a percentage as a complete description. The two assessments sample related domains, but their difficulty has not been statistically equated. Different item wording and production demands can influence results, so the report explicitly limits what its counts imply.
advanced: Integrated tasks can reveal gaps hidden by isolated recognition. A learner may select a correct modal in a gap yet remove uncertainty while writing a summary, or identify an object complement yet introduce a dangling opening during compression. Check form, function and intended interpretation together. A meaning-preserving correction should retain actors, time, quantity and logical relations; a formal alternative may change emphasis without being a required repair. Your written response can differ from the model if it meets the stated criteria. Explain that difference where a regional, register or terminology choice is relevant.
expert: Mastery in the title names the aim of continuing development, not a certificate awarded by finishing thirty lessons. Evidence remains conditional on the tasks sampled, the amount of previous exposure and the reliability of self-review. Objective counts concern keyed items; an independent paragraph requires separate attention to grammatical accuracy, meaning, organisation and audience. If feedback was consulted before a response, record that limitation rather than presenting the response as unaided. A stronger capstone performance can justify a more challenging next task, but it does not prove complete control of every construction or predict an official examination result.

patterns.form: comparable domain + different item → cautious comparison
patterns.meaning: Related content supports reflection, while unequal difficulty limits numerical conclusions.

patterns.form: original response → rubric comparison → reasoned self-review
patterns.meaning: Keeps production separate from model exposure.

examples.sentence: Diagnostic: two of four article items correct; capstone: three of four correct.
examples.analysis: This is a difference on the sampled items, not a statistically calibrated article-proficiency gain.

examples.sentence: A learner selects might correctly but writes the result will occur in a summary of a possible outcome.
examples.analysis: Recognition and meaning-preserving production provide different evidence.

examples.sentence: The final draft uses a passive to retain the instrument as topic.
examples.analysis: A justified discourse choice need not be replaced merely to increase the number of active verbs.

contrasts.b: I can independently use every English construction.
contrasts.note: The first records completion; the second is a much broader claim that this assessment cannot establish.

exceptions: A lower count in one domain can result from a more demanding sample. Inspect the actual errors and responses before interpreting it as a general loss of knowledge.

mistakes.problem: Four correct repeated answers equal four new independent items.
mistakes.repair: Four responses to a previously exposed item remain responses to one item.
mistakes.reason: The comparison must account for item exposure.

mistakes.problem: A high multiple-choice count proves that my paragraph is accurate.
mistakes.repair: Review the paragraph separately for its grammatical and meaning criteria.
mistakes.reason: Recognition does not objectively grade original production.

glossary.definition: An integrated final task connecting previously studied abilities.
glossary.example: A report combines grammatical choices, editing and reference management.

glossary.definition: Establishing comparable measurement properties through appropriate evidence.
glossary.example: These instructional difficulty labels are not calibrated test scores.

modules.title: Turn the topic profile into a specific continuing revision plan
modules.definition: A useful revision plan links a demonstrated difficulty to an explanation, a fresh application and a later retrieval opportunity. It responds to the evidence available rather than assigning an unsupported global proficiency label.
foundation: Start with a precise description of the difficulty. Articles is a broad area; confusing indefinite introduction with identifiable reference is a usable revision target. Find the relevant lesson and reference entry, then explain the distinction beside two examples. Next attempt a different task that requires applying it. If the weakness concerns original writing, write a new short passage and inspect every relevant choice. Reading a lesson may improve understanding, but record it as study rather than as proof that the next unfamiliar use will be accurate.
intermediate: Prioritise recurring unresolved errors without ignoring new topics. An agreement problem caused by intervening phrases calls for subject analysis; a problem involving collectives also requires interpretation and variety. Do not apply one repair mechanically to both. Use the scheduled retrieval dates to revisit an item after an interval, and keep the original response in the record. A same-day retry after feedback is useful practice, but it should not become an additional spaced success. When a remembered item becomes easy, add a new context or a written explanation instead of relying exclusively on repetition.
advanced: Use separate evidence streams when deciding what to do next. First-response recognition can indicate a distinction needing explanation; repeated retrieval can show retention of that sampled item; correction and transformation reveal how well you preserve relationships; original writing shows whether you can coordinate several choices at once. Self-review labels are your own judgements against a rubric. If a response remains uncertain, record the exact question, consult a reliable source and identify whether the uncertainty concerns grammar, region, register, style or intended meaning. An unfamiliar standard form should not be classified as an error merely to make the report appear decisive.
expert: A personalised plan can be modest and explicit. Select two priority concepts, schedule one unfamiliar response task for each, and set a separate extended-writing session. After reviewing that work, revise the plan using the new evidence. The number of days is a planning choice, not a promise about how quickly every learner acquires grammatical control. Preserve earlier samples so that improvement can be examined rather than reconstructed from memory. A strong plan also includes maintenance of areas that currently look secure and occasional work on unsampled constructions; absence of a recorded error is not evidence that a topic has been exhaustively tested.

patterns.form: observed difficulty → precise distinction → fresh task

patterns.meaning: Allows improvement without rewriting the baseline.

examples.sentence: Target: I add a pronoun inside an object relative.
examples.analysis: Review the gap in the report that I requested, then construct three new object relatives.

examples.sentence: Target: I change may to will during compression.
examples.analysis: Compare the force of the two modals and write a summary retaining possibility.

examples.sentence: A scheduled item is answered correctly after two separated retrieval opportunities.
examples.analysis: This is evidence about retention of that item, alongside rather than in place of independent writing.

contrasts.b: On Wednesday, explain object-relative gaps and combine four new sentence pairs.
contrasts.note: The second specifies a concept, an observable task and a review occasion.

exceptions: A learner with no recorded objective errors still needs unfamiliar production tasks. A clean notebook can reflect a small sample or little practice rather than complete proficiency.

mistakes.problem: My notebook is empty, so no further study is necessary.
mistakes.repair: Check what has been sampled and attempt new production where evidence is limited.
mistakes.reason: No recorded error is not an exhaustive test.

mistakes.problem: I should review every topic for the same length of time regardless of evidence.
mistakes.repair: Give priority to demonstrated gaps while retaining a manageable maintenance schedule.
mistakes.reason: A plan should respond to observed needs without permanently excluding other areas.

glossary.definition: Study directed at a specified distinction or recurring problem.
glossary.example: Article identifiability rather than all nouns.

glossary.definition: A later performance relevant to remembered material.
glossary.example: A spaced correct response to a previously missed item.

modules.title: Use the permanent reference and continue beyond the thirty-day path
modules.definition: A permanent grammar reference is a topic-organised resource for consultation and deeper study. The structured course is one route through it; completing the route does not end access or remove the need for continued reading, production and revision.
foundation: Use the reference index to answer a real grammatical question. If a sentence contains an unfamiliar noun phrase, begin with the noun-phrase entry and its terminology, then follow prerequisite explanations as needed. The glossary supplies short definitions and examples; the full entry explains patterns, restrictions and contrasts. A quick rule can orient you, but a context-dependent question may require the deeper layer. Bookmark an entry when it helps with a recurring problem and write a note stating the distinction in your own words, rather than copying an isolated prohibition.
intermediate: Choose a continuing practice route that matches the question. The sentence analysis lab helps identify structures and functions. The transformation lab asks whether a requested change preserves time, participants and meaning. The correction and editing lab includes suspicious but grammatical examples, so leaving a form unchanged can be a reasoned answer. The usage guide compares established regional and register alternatives. Formal-writing practice connects grammar with qualification, cohesion and economy. These resources overlap deliberately through shared concepts; they are not different courses that a learner must complete separately.
advanced: Keep reading and original production connected. Select a sentence from a text you are entitled to use, analyse its structure and imitate the pattern with new content. Do not assume that every published sentence illustrates the same register or editorial convention. When a source and a remembered rule conflict, check the grammatical context and the authority’s scope. A dictionary can resolve a lexical pattern; a broader grammar may be needed for syntactic analysis; a style guide can identify a house convention. Distinguish these purposes rather than turning a publisher’s preference into an absolute rule of English.
expert: Continuing development should include deliberate contact with unfamiliar contexts and independent written expression. A more technical analysis is useful when it explains a real contrast, but added terminology is not itself better writing. Conversely, a beginner-friendly explanation should remain compatible with its advanced qualification. Return to foundation layers when a prerequisite is unclear and open expert extensions when the deeper distinction matters. Keep saved drafts and earlier assessments as evidence of the work completed. The continuing goal is accurate, context-sensitive control: selecting a grammatical construction for the meaning and audience required, then being able to defend or revise that choice with appropriate evidence.

patterns.meaning: Uses reference material to resolve an actual learning need.

patterns.form: analyse a pattern → create new content → check meaning
patterns.meaning: Connects reference study with original production.

examples.sentence: A writer is unsure whether team can take are.
examples.analysis: Consult collective agreement and regional interpretation rather than applying a blanket singular rule.

examples.sentence: A writer wants to reduce a report by forty words.
examples.analysis: Check compression, reference and modality; preserve qualifications before deleting wording.

examples.sentence: A learner analyses an unfamiliar embedded question and writes a different one.
examples.analysis: The new production tests whether the structural relationship can be transferred beyond a memorised example.

contrasts.a: A style guide prefers one quotation convention.
contrasts.b: Every other quotation convention is grammatically wrong.
contrasts.note: The first can state a legitimate house preference; the second wrongly converts that preference into a universal law.

exceptions: A short note or conversational answer may legitimately omit material that a formal standalone paragraph needs. Consultation must take genre and context into account.

mistakes.problem: The thirty days are finished, so access to review should end.
mistakes.repair: Continue using the lessons, reference entries and practice opportunities as needed.
mistakes.reason: The schedule organises learning rather than setting a limit on access.

mistakes.problem: A longer grammatical label automatically improves my sentence.
mistakes.repair: Use technical analysis when it clarifies a distinction, and revise prose for the intended reader.
mistakes.reason: Terminology and communicative quality are related but not identical achievements.

glossary.definition: A substantial topic explanation available for consultation.
glossary.example: An article entry explains generic and identifiable reference.

glossary.definition: Applying a learned distinction in a different context.
glossary.example: Using a relative clause accurately in a newly written paragraph.

questions.prompt: In The librarian gave the visitor a receipt, which phrase is the indirect object?
questions.why: The visitor is the recipient indirect object; a receipt is the direct object and The librarian is the subject.

questions.prompt: In teacher + -s, what does the final -s express?
options: A change from noun to adjective
questions.why: The suffix marks grammatical number on the noun teachers. It does not create a different word class.

questions.prompt: What is the head of these remarkably accurate measurements of rainfall?
questions.why: Measurements heads the whole noun phrase. Rainfall heads the smaller noun phrase inside the of-phrase.

questions.prompt: In an analysis of the archive report, which quoted expression has non-finite verb structure?
options: Did the archivist check the index?
whether the archivist checked the index
questions.why: To check the revised index is an infinitival non-finite clause. The other expressions contain finite verb structure.

questions.prompt: The mentor offered three useful ____ of advice.
questions.why: Pieces is a countable plural unit compatible with three. Advice stays uncountable in this ordinary general sense.

questions.prompt: Introduce one unidentified Member of Parliament using the spoken initials /em piː/: ____ MP attended the meeting.
questions.why: MP begins with a vowel sound when pronounced as initials, so an is the appropriate indefinite article.

questions.prompt: A colleague uses they as their personal pronoun. Which sentence respects that pronoun choice and ordinary agreement?
questions.why: Singular they ordinarily retains the verb forms used with they, including are. The singular referent does not require is.

questions.prompt: Several children jointly use the room. Which possessive is standard?
questions.why: Children is an irregular plural without final s, so the possessive adds apostrophe + s.

questions.prompt: The courier ____ the parcel last Tuesday and then left.
options: has been delivered, with courier as agent
questions.why: The completed delivery is placed in a finished past period by last Tuesday. Past simple delivered fits the narrative.

questions.prompt: Choose the present-perfect passive corresponding to The technician has checked the alarms.
options: The alarms had check by the technician.
The alarms have been checked by the technician.
The alarms has checked by the technician.
The alarms have being checked by the technician.
questions.why: Have been checked preserves present perfect and adds passive be + past participle, with plural agreement for alarms.

questions.prompt: The speaker is uncertain, not imposing a duty: The lights are off; the staff might be upstairs. What does might express?
questions.why: Might presents a possibility based on the available situation. It does not impose a requirement or prohibition.

questions.prompt: Complete the established pattern: The organisers avoided ____ the two appointments.
questions.why: Avoid normally selects an -ing complement in this intended meaning: avoided overlapping.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses an object relative without repeating its object?
options: The guide that we consulted was helpful.
The guide that we consulted it was helpful.
The guide which we consulted it was helpful.
The guide whom we consulted was helpful, when guide means a book.
questions.why: The relative marker corresponds to the object of consulted, so the object is not repeated as it. The context explicitly makes guide a book rather than a person.

questions.prompt: Replace the object with a pronoun: Please put away the folders.
questions.why: With this separable phrasal verb, an unstressed object pronoun normally occurs between verb and particle: put them away.

questions.prompt: Which sentence explicitly compares one building’s energy use with another building’s energy use?
options: This building’s energy use is lower than that of the next building.
This building’s energy use is lower than expensive buildings.
This building’s energy use is lower than the next building is old.
This building’s energy use is lower than the next building.
questions.why: That of the next building identifies its energy use, producing a logically parallel comparison.

questions.prompt: Lina is intended to have examined the chart. Which version explicitly preserves that interpretation?
options: After Lina examined the chart, the discrepancy surprised her.
Having examined the chart, the discrepancy was surprising.
To examine the chart, the discrepancy appeared large.
After examining the chart, the discrepancy surprised Lina.
questions.why: The finite after-clause names Lina as examiner. The main clause then states the discrepancy’s effect on her without assigning examination to the discrepancy.

questions.prompt: Which version uses a semicolon to join two complete related main clauses?
options: The hearing; ended the witnesses left.
The hearing ended; because the room closed.
The hearing ended the; witnesses left.
The hearing ended; the witnesses left.
questions.why: The first version places a complete main clause on each side of the semicolon. The other placements interrupt structure or do not provide the requested pair.

questions.prompt: Which editorial judgement is defensible?
options: Every American spelling is a grammatical error in English.
Established British and American spellings can both be standard; a publication may choose a consistent convention.
British English always requires -ize and never permits -ise.
A spelling preference proves that a sentence has the wrong subject.
questions.why: Established regional spelling alternatives should be distinguished from grammar errors. Consistent editorial choices can be appropriate without invalidating other standard conventions.

questions.prompt: The archive has revised ____ opening hours.
questions.why: Its is the possessive determiner. Expanding it’s as it is or it has does not fit this noun phrase.

questions.prompt: The revised fee had an immediate ____ on demand.
questions.why: The noun effect fits after an immediate and before on. The specialised noun affect does not carry the intended result meaning here.

questions.prompt: Only twelve volunteers answered a survey: nine supported the change and three opposed it. Which claim is appropriately limited to that evidence?
options: The volunteers’ replies suggest support within that small responding group.
The entire town has certainly changed its view.
questions.why: The selected claim identifies the limited responding group and uses suggest rather than making an unsupported universal or certain conclusion.

questions.prompt: A report mentions both a damaged scanner and a delayed delivery. Which continuation explicitly identifies the scanner as what was replaced?
options: This was replaced, with no other identifying context.
It was replaced, with no other identifying context.
questions.why: Repeating the scanner removes the competing reference and states the replacement clearly. It or this may be recoverable in some contexts, but the question requires explicit identification.

questions.prompt: Original: Some rural libraries may extend their hours if the pilot is funded. Which summary preserves the main qualifications?
options: Some rural libraries may open longer if the pilot receives funding.
Rural libraries have extended their hours permanently.
Funding has increased because every library opens longer.
questions.why: The selected version preserves limited quantity, rural scope, possibility and the funding condition. The others change certainty, time, coverage or logical relationship.

questions.prompt: Original: The laboratory may repeat the test after the equipment is repaired. Which revision preserves the commitment and sequence?
options: After the equipment is repaired, the laboratory may repeat the test.
The laboratory will certainly repeat the test before the equipment is repaired.
The equipment was repaired because the test was repeated.
Every laboratory must repeat all tests.
questions.why: The selected revision changes ordering of the clauses without changing possibility or the repair-before-repetition sequence. The other versions add or reverse important content.

questions.prompt: In The research team will sample the water, classify research, team and sample in their contexts and identify research’s function.
questions.model: Research is a noun functioning as a premodifier; team is the noun head of the subject phrase; sample is a plain-form lexical verb after will.
rubric: Keep word class distinct from modifier or subject function.
Use the sentence context to distinguish sample as verb from its noun use elsewhere.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Choose ordinary formal agreement in the stated readings: Forty per cent of the water ____ contaminated, but forty per cent of the samples ____ safe. Use past forms of be.
questions.model: Forty per cent of the water was contaminated, but forty per cent of the samples were safe.
rubric: Use singular agreement with uncountable water and plural agreement with samples.
Do not make the percentage word alone determine number.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Contrast The hall has been empty for a year and The hall was empty for a year, using normal independent-clause readings.
questions.model: The present perfect normally connects the year-long state to now. The past simple locates a year-long state in a past period and does not by itself assert that it continues now. Context can add a later situation.
rubric: Distinguish connection to now from a past period.
Avoid claiming that the simple past logically proves the hall is occupied now.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Explain two possible reports of a still-current timetable after The manager said: the train leaves at six / the train left at six.
questions.model: The present can retain the timetable as currently true from the reporter’s perspective. The past can be ordinary backshift in a past report and need not mean the timetable has ceased to apply. The surrounding context selects the intended temporal perspective.
rubric: Allow retained present and ordinary backshift where the context supports each.
Do not infer that backshift necessarily makes the information false now.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Explain the likely reference difference between The volunteers who arrived early helped set up and The volunteers, who arrived early, helped set up.
questions.model: Without commas the relative helps identify the subset of volunteers. With commas it supplements an identified group and normally presents early arrival as applying to that group.
rubric: Discuss restriction versus supplementary information.
Do not describe the commas as meaningless decoration.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Give two established formal mandative completions of The board recommended that she ... using attend, and distinguish them from an assertion about what she actually does.
questions.model: The board recommended that she attend. / The board recommended that she should attend. Both can express a recommendation rather than assert that she actually attends. Plain subjunctive attend and mandative should are established alternatives, with regional/style preferences.
rubric: Use plain attend in the subjunctive rather than attends.
Recognise British mandative should as legitimate.
Explain recommendation versus factual assertion.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Explain why They slept in this bed can license This bed was slept in, while The guests arrived cannot become The guests were arrived in ordinary standard English.
questions.model: The prepositional construction sleep in can license a passive whose subject corresponds to the complement of in. Ordinary intransitive arrive does not license the proposed be-passive. Passive possibilities depend on the lexical construction and its argument relationships, not merely on the presence of any verb.
rubric: Identify the prepositional passive and retained in.
Explain why the arrive proposal is restricted without claiming that every intransitive-looking construction behaves alike.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Identify the understood editor in Salma tried to edit the draft and Salma persuaded Nadia to edit the draft. Explain the control contrast.
questions.model: In the try construction, Salma is understood as the editor and is the person making the effort. In the persuade construction, Nadia is understood as the editor. The first illustrates subject control; the second illustrates object control. These interpretations follow the lexical patterns rather than a rule that simply selects the nearest noun.
rubric: Identify Salma versus Nadia as the understood subject.
Use the control labels consistently with those interpretations.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Arrange every supplied token once into the ordinary negative-inversion pattern: such / we / have / never / seen / precision. Do not add words.
questions.model: Never have we seen such precision.
rubric: Place fronted never before inverted have we.
Keep seen as the past participle and use all supplied tokens.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Use a wh-cleft to focus the needed resource: We need more reliable evidence.
questions.model: What we need is more reliable evidence.
rubric: Use what we need as the initial fused-relative/wh-cleft unit.
Retain the need for more reliable evidence and acknowledge the shift in focus.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Combine using although, preserving the concession: The route was longer. It was easier to navigate.
questions.model: Although the route was longer, it was easier to navigate.
rubric: Retain the longer route and easier navigation facts.
Use although to mark concession, not an unsupported cause.
alternatives: The route was easier to navigate although it was longer.

questions.prompt: Split into two complete sentences without changing the participants or chronology: When the clock struck noon, the assistants closed the desk and the visitors left.
questions.model: The clock struck noon. At that time, the assistants closed the desk and the visitors left.
rubric: Retain the noon time frame and both main events.
Use complete sentences and preserve the intended sequence without inventing a reason.
alternatives: The assistants closed the desk when the clock struck noon. The visitors left at that time. Other two-sentence versions must retain the clock event as well as both main events.

questions.prompt: Explain how one differs from did so in The red folder is damaged; use the blue one and She promised to inspect the valve and did so.
questions.model: One substitutes for a countable noun within the noun phrase, here a blue folder. Did so substitutes for the inspection action. The two substitutes are not interchangeable merely because both avoid repetition.
rubric: Identify the size and type of unit replaced.
Do not replace a noun with did so or an action with one in these constructions.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Edit genuine grammar and boundary errors while keeping every fact: The new labels was printed on Monday. The boxes were checked, however, two labels was missing. The supervisor asked where had the spare labels been stored.
questions.model: The new labels were printed on Monday. The boxes were checked; however, two labels were missing. The supervisor asked where the spare labels had been stored.
rubric: Repair plural labels/were in both places.
Repair the boundary before connective however.
Use statement order within the embedded interrogative while preserving its past-perfect passive.
alternatives: A full stop before However is also valid.

questions.prompt: Source: During a three-week trial, visits rose. The trial coincided with a local festival, and its independent effect was not measured. Explain why The trial caused visits to rise is not a faithful précis.
questions.model: The source reports a rise during the trial, not an isolated causal effect. The festival is a competing circumstance and the independent effect was not measured. A faithful summary could say that visits rose during the trial, while its causal contribution remained uncertain.
rubric: Distinguish temporal association from asserted cause.
Retain the confounding circumstance or the explicit uncertainty it creates.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Write 80–100 words explaining a cautious recommendation about a study or workplace procedure. Include a condition and a clear reference chain; mark those features after writing.
questions.model:
The department could test the revised filing procedure for one month if staff can maintain both versions during the trial. The new system may reduce the time needed to locate older records, but that benefit has not yet been measured. Staff should record search times and report any missing documents. Their reports would help the manager compare the two procedures before choosing a permanent arrangement. If the new version creates additional errors, the department should revise it rather than assume that a faster search is the only important outcome.

Annotation: if staff can maintain supplies a condition; the department/the new system/staff/their reports/the manager form traceable references.
rubric: Produce 80–100 words before the annotation.
Use an appropriate condition and cautious commitment.
Make reference recoverable and retain any limitations on the recommendation.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct genuine errors: The adviser gave us several useful advices.
corrections.model: The adviser gave us several useful pieces of advice.
rubric: Retain the several separate items intended.
Use ordinary uncountable advice without a plural ending.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct ordinary coordinated-object case: The tutor spoke to Hamza and I.
corrections.model: The tutor spoke to Hamza and me.
rubric: Use objective case in the complement of to.
Preserve Hamza and the speaker as the people addressed.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct the standard auxiliary pattern: She did not submitted the application.
corrections.model: She did not submit the application.
rubric: Keep past do-support.
Use plain submit after did not.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct genuine errors: The number of incomplete forms have fallen.
corrections.model: The number of incomplete forms has fallen.
rubric: Treat the number as the singular head in this figure reading.
Preserve present-perfect meaning.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Revise for the intended manner meaning: The witness answered the question confident. Intended: confidently describes how the witness answered; the task is not to add a separate description of the witness’s state.
corrections.model: The witness answered the question confidently.
rubric: Use an adverb for the intended manner of answering.
Do not replace the witness or the event.
An adjective can describe a subject’s state in a licensed depictive construction; do not infer a universal ban on adjectives after action verbs.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct genuine errors in ordinary edited relative structure: The permit that I requested it arrived yesterday.
corrections.model: The permit that I requested arrived yesterday.
rubric: Leave the relative object position unfilled by a repeated it.
Retain the permit’s arrival yesterday.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct the embedded question: We asked whether was the entrance accessible.
corrections.model: We asked whether the entrance was accessible.
rubric: Use statement word order after whether.
Retain the yes/no content and past reference.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Nadia is the intended speaker of the opening words. Repair Speaking to the registrar, the delay worried Nadia.
corrections.model: While Nadia was speaking to the registrar, the delay worried her.
rubric: Name Nadia as the speaker in an explicit finite clause.
Retain the fact that the delay worried Nadia.
alternatives: Speaking to the registrar, Nadia was worried about the delay.

corrections.prompt: Correct only genuine errors: This is the room which we booked for the meeting.
corrections.model: No change is required: This is the room which we booked for the meeting.
rubric: Recognise established restrictive which in standard English.
Do not impose an optional house preference for that as a universal grammar rule.
alternatives: This is the room that we booked for the meeting is also a valid alternative.

corrections.prompt: Correct only genuine errors in ordinary standard English: Which desk did you leave the forms on?

rubric: Recognise standard preposition stranding.
Retain the question about the desk’s identity.
alternatives: On which desk did you leave the forms? is a more formal alternative.

transformations.prompt: Make passive and retain the agent and past perfect: The surveyors had marked the unsafe path.

transformations.prompt: Nominalise approve without deleting the named agent: The committee approved the plan, and this approval surprised the contractors. Rewrite the first event as a noun phrase that is the subject of one clause.
transformations.model: The committee’s approval of the plan surprised the contractors.
rubric: Keep the committee as approver and the plan as what was approved.
Preserve the contractors’ reaction without inventing a reason.
alternatives: The approval of the plan by the committee surprised the contractors.

writing.prompt:
Complete BOTH tasks using the original case passage below. 1. Write a180–220-word formal report explaining what the evidence supports and recommending a cautious next step. Include a condition, a passive, an accurately attributed finding and clear reference. 2. Write a65–80-word précis preserving the principal limitations and conditions. Do not turn association, interviews or initial visit totals into proof of universal benefit.

A community archive tested Saturday opening for six weeks during the spring term. It recorded 120 visits, but the register counted visits rather than individual people, so the total number of different visitors was unknown. Ten visitors volunteered for short interviews. Eight said that Saturday opening was convenient, while two reported difficulties with weekend transport. The interviewees were not selected to represent all users, and the archive did not interview people who had been unable to attend. Weekday opening hours remained unchanged throughout the trial.

Staff welcomed the opportunity to speak with visitors who worked during the week, but they did not keep a separate record of the trial’s staffing costs. They also warned that a quieter period might produce a different pattern of demand. The manager therefore proposed collecting more information before any permanent change. A longer trial could compare attendance in different months and record both costs and reasons for missed visits. Any extension would depend on adequate funding and enough volunteers to cover the additional shifts. The present figures were intended as initial evidence for a decision, not proof that permanent Saturday opening would benefit every user.
writing.model:
1. One formal report (202 words):
The archive’s six-week Saturday-opening trial provides useful initial evidence, but it does not yet justify a permanent change. Staff recorded 120 visits during the spring term. Because the register counted visits rather than individual people, the number of different visitors remains unknown. Eight of the ten voluntary interviewees welcomed Saturday opening, while two reported transport difficulties. Their views cannot be treated as representative of all users, particularly because people unable to attend were not interviewed.

A longer trial could help the manager examine demand in different months if funding and volunteers are available. Weekday opening should remain unchanged while that work is carried out. The extended review should record staffing costs, unique visitors where appropriate and reasons for missed visits. It should also distinguish a quiet month from evidence that the service has no value.

The present findings do not guarantee that every user would benefit from permanent Saturday hours. However, a carefully documented extension may provide a firmer basis for the decision. If the additional shifts cannot be staffed without weakening existing services, the archive should postpone expansion and consider another limited arrangement. Any recommendation should retain these practical conditions rather than treating the first visit total as proof of success.

2. One précis (67 words):
During a six-week Saturday-opening trial, a community archive recorded 120 visits, but the number of different visitors was unknown. Eight of ten voluntary interviewees welcomed the hours; two reported transport difficulties, so their views cannot represent all users. Weekday hours remained unchanged. Because staffing costs were unrecorded and future demand is uncertain, a longer trial should precede permanent adoption. Any extension depends on sufficient funding and volunteers.

Annotation: if funding and volunteers are available states a condition; cannot be treated/while that work is carried out are passive patterns in the report; the interview views are attributed to the ten volunteers rather than all users. The précis retains the visit/person distinction, unrepresentative interviews, unchanged weekday hours, unrecorded costs, uncertainty and extension conditions.
rubric: Task 1: produce 180–220 words and retain the evidence limits, including the difference between visits and individual visitors.
Task 1: use clear reference, a condition, a passive and accurate attribution; do not invent measured costs or universal preferences.
Task 2: produce 65–80 words and preserve the major qualifications, uncertainty and funding/staffing conditions.
Compare both pieces with the original meaning and the rubric; record independent writing separately from the objective score.
alternatives: Other reports may recommend a different cautious action if it follows from the supplied facts. Other précis wording is acceptable if it preserves the main argument and qualifications within the stated length.

recall.prompt: Compare one diagnostic and one capstone response in a shared skill domain. State what changed and one limit on the comparison. If either was unanswered, state that limitation instead of inventing a gain.
recall.model: Example reflection: In the diagnostic I treated an entire noun phrase as if only its head could be the subject. In the capstone I identified the whole phrase and then named its head. This is evidence of a better analysis on these examples, but the items were different and the result is not a calibrated overall proficiency gain.
rubric: Use actual personal responses when available.
Name the grammatical distinction rather than only a percentage.
Acknowledge missing responses or different item difficulty where relevant.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

recall.prompt: Create a one-week continuing plan for two precise weak concepts and one original-writing task. Include a later retrieval occasion without promising mastery by the end of the week.
recall.model: Monday: review object-relative gaps and combine four unfamiliar sentence pairs. Wednesday: contrast may, must and might in evidence-based claims and explain three new contexts. Friday: write a150-word report using both areas, then compare it with the relevant rubrics. On the scheduled retrieval dates, revisit the earlier missed items without treating repeats as new questions. Adjust the plan after inspecting the new writing.
rubric: Specify two distinctions and fresh applications.
Include original connected writing and a later retrieval occasion.
Keep improvement evidence separate from a guaranteed mastery deadline.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

recall.prompt: Choose a continuing resource for each need: (a) identify an unfamiliar phrase’s head; (b) preserve modality in a précis; (c) check a British/American difference. Explain the choice.
recall.model: (a) Use phrase structure and the sentence analysis lab to identify the head and hierarchy. (b) Use the précis/formal-writing material and modality reference to retain the force of may, must or other commitments. (c) Use the variation guide and an appropriate authoritative entry to distinguish regional convention from an error.
rubric: Match each resource to the actual question.
Explain why a quick unqualified rule may be insufficient.
Do not invent an official preference when checking regional alternatives.
alternatives: A different formulation is valid if it preserves the stated meaning and fulfils the specific structural requirements.

checklist: I completed the capstone before consulting its models where possible, and recorded any help used.
I preserved meaning and legitimate standard alternatives during correction.
I compared my original report and précis with the stated criteria, not an exact model string.
I interpreted diagnostic and capstone counts as limited samples rather than certified proficiency.
I selected specific continuing tasks and know that the full course remains open.
